newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says could use confidence votes on budget.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says could use confidence votes on budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi was quoted on Friday as saying his government could resort to confidence votes to get Italy's 1997 budget through parliament if a mountain of amendments holds up its passage.

In an interview with the newspaper La Repubblica, Prodi also said he hoped gross domestic product (GDP) would grow by 2.0 percent in 1997 and said he saw no reason for inflation, now running at around 3.0 percent year-on-year, to rise.

The 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) budget, drawn up to try to help Italy make the grade for membership of Europe's planned single currency, goes before the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) next Wednesday and a final vote is due by mid-November.
"If there is a huge pile of amendments, I think the answer is yes," Prodi said when asked if his centre-left government would use confidence votes to sweep aside proposed change.
"It depends on how responsible the opposition is."

Prodi has used confidence votes twice since his appointment in May, most recently this week when he won such a motion to remove 1,001 amendments presented by the separatist Northern League party to a decree on a rescue plan for the ailing southern bank, Banco di Napoli.
The centre-right opposition Freedom Alliance and the League have also presented a welter of amendments to the budget and insisted on full debate.

The budget faces its toughest ride in the lowest house, where Prodi depends on external support from the hard left party Communist Refoundation for his government's majority. He has control of the Senate, where the budget goes next.
Prodi said he expected the budget, which is heavy on revenue-raising measures, to have a "minimal depressive effect" but that it would not spark an economic recession.

"I have done my sums and can say that the government's budget will not impact the structure of consumption," he said. "The highest cost is uncertainty, the sense of uncertainty there is in the country."
He said a European economic recovery was now under way and there were positive signals in Italy. "The fall is over," he said.
On inflation, he said he saw "no reason why it should start rising again".
The Bank of Italy on Wednesday cut its key discount rate by 75 basis points to 7.50 percent after signs that official consumer price inflation in October would drop to 3.0 percent.
